body:
> The changes made in this PR seem to have a performance regression but I am not sure if it stems from my benchmarking method or uints having characteristics that I don't know of. Please let me know if I there is something wrong with my method.

If it has measurable performance issues it shouldn't be changed at least not like this, they should be fixed or the changes shouldn't be made IMO, unless there's some benefit from this other than modernization

Why the change to uint32_t from int?

> Why the change to uint32_t from int?

Other containers also use `(u)int*_t`s instead of plain `int`s, so it would be good for consistency and there is no reason for these values to be signed anyway as they hold indexes.

Logically, this shouldn't cause any major performance regressions but there is an undeniable one. Unless there is something I don't know about unsigned values, the only logical explainations are either my benchmark is broken or the compiler was able to generate better code with signed values than it could with unsigned ones.

I originally was aiming to make this PR with much more changes, but after seeing regressions on that one, I reverted those changes and opted to only converting `int`s. But the exact same regressions happened again, and I actually want to find out why this happens. So I would be very happy if people that are knowledgeable about performance and benchmarking to take a look at why this might be the case.

While i appreciate the effort and would probably do something similar in personal projects, please note that modernization for modernization's sake is not sufficient motivation for changes to Godot. 
Our pull requests should be informed by bug fixes, performance enhancements or feature requests - a tangible benefit.

We do want to avoid the use of `int` in new code, but i wouldn't advocate for going through the codebase to exchange them just for that.

> Other containers also use (u)int*_ts instead of plain ints, so it would be good for consistency and there is no reason for these values to be signed anyway as they hold indexes.

But you are changing `int` to `uint32_t` instead of `int32_t`, and most other containers use `intX_t` for indices, like `Vector`, `List`, `VSet`, `Array`, `Dictionary`, and `String`

> While i appreciate the effort and would probably do something similar in personal projects, please note that modernization for modernization's sake is not sufficient motivation for changes to Godot. Our pull requests should be informed by bug fixes, performance enhancements or feature requests - a tangible benefit.

A stance that I not only understand but also support. I should have opened this as a draft anyway; it is a mistake on my part.

> We do want to avoid the use of `int` in new code, but i wouldn't advocate for going through the codebase to exchange them just for that.

Like I mentioned in my previous comment, I was actually aiming for bigger changes, including both perf and readability improvements, and then tunnel visioned to this weird regression. I probably should create another PR that has the other improvements without the uint part.

> But you are changing int to uint32_t instead of int32_t, and most other containers use intX_t for indices, like Vector, List, VSet, Array, Dictionary, and String

I don't know why the mentioned containers don't use `uint*_t`s and opt for signed ones, but RingBuffer doesn't really need to use a signed one, just like its inner container `LocalVector`. In this case, the only reason to use a signed value over an unsigned one is that GCC seems to do (or not do) some gimmicks (see: *Edit* at the benchmark section).

I will be converting this to a draft until I find a fix/workaround to this regression. Can close if requested.

I'd say changing to `int32_t`, if it doesn't cause performance regressions, would be acceptable, though it won't do much more than improve clarity, but changing to `uint32_t` should only be done if there's some good reason, it risks causing unexpected issues and regressions due to the change, it also breaks the established patterns of most types

I also don't think `uint32_t` makes any sense as an index for this type as it uses `-1` to indicate invalid indices, like several of the other container types that do this, mixing sign for that is confusing, the fact that you need to cast the result of `find` to `uint32_t` to use it in other methods at least for full correctness is weird IMO
